tldr: In decentralized robot swarms, training each robot independently to predict the same latent future target (JEPA) without any explicit agreement loss substantially improves both prediction agreement across robots and physical prediction accuracy at the same time.
overview:
For robot swarms to coordinate effectively, having a shared outlook on what the whole team is becoming is essential. In a fully decentralized setting, however, each robot only sees fragmented evidence from itself and its immediate neighbors. They cannot rely on a central server, nor can they aggregate or average their predictions at runtime. As a result, when individual robots predict the future independently, they often imagine mutually conflicting futures, causing coordination to break down.

The authors hypothesize that compatible, meaningful predictions can emerge naturally without forcing robots into an explicit agreement loss, as long as every robot is self-supervised to predict the exact same abstract latent future. To achieve this, they introduce Collective-State JEPA (CS-JEPA). Using a fixed-width token design where communication bandwidth and target representation size remain constant even as the swarm grows, CS-JEPA trains robots to predict key collective latent states rather than reconstructing the raw sensory details of observations.

Evaluation spans communication topology shifts, scaling out to swarms up to 6x larger than seen during training, linear probing with extremely scarce labels, and decentralized rigid-body control of Crazyflie drones. Compared to a capacity-matched baseline that reconstructs raw observations, CS-JEPA slashes collective-state error by 64.4 to 75.6% under unseen topologies and swarm-size shifts, while improving prediction agreement across all random seeds without explicit consensus training. This work clearly shows that even from fragmented local evidence, decentralized robots can align their awareness through a shared latent future.
contributions: Proposed Collective-State JEPA (CS-JEPA), a size-invariant shared latent future prediction architecture that keeps communication bandwidth and representation dimensions constant as swarm size grows
Demonstrated through rigorous independent replications that prediction agreement and physical accuracy improve simultaneously, even with zero agreement loss encouraging predictions to match
Achieved strong generalization to unseen communication topologies and swarm sizes up to 6x larger than training, along with accurate collective-state decoding using minimal labels (e.g., 6 episodes)
Showed that receiver-local representations directly benefit independent decision-making in counterfactual value estimation and fully decentralized rigid-body Crazyflie drone control

sections.heading: How can decentralized robots align on the future without consensus?
sections.summary: Decentralized robots often form conflicting future predictions because each robot only has access to local information. This paper investigates whether CS-JEPA can foster compatible collective-state predictions spontaneously by predicting a shared latent future without central consensus or output pooling.
sections.details:
When a swarm of robots flocks, splits, or rotates, no single robot can directly observe the macroscopic state of the entire swarm. Each robot only receives fragmented evidence—its own observations and bounded messages from neighbors. Because of this, even if every robot forms a plausible prediction, they can arrive at mutually incompatible pictures of the future, leading to a failure mode unique to decentralized systems.

Prior work has explored recovering global structure from local communication, multi-agent representation learning, and world models. Recently, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) have gained attention by predicting in a learned feature space (latent space) rather than reconstructing fine sensory details. However, whether predicting a latent collective target without explicit agreement losses can align independent predictions across robots—and whether that holds under topology and swarm-size shifts—remained open.

The core intuition of CS-JEPA is that if robots with different local viewpoints are trained to predict the same latent future, the meanings of those viewpoints will naturally align. Crucially, if robots simply collapse to outputting a constant value, agreement would be 100% while being completely uninformative. Thus, one must prove that prediction agreement and physical state estimation accuracy improve at the same time. This study rigorously tests this question both theoretically and empirically.

sections.heading: From local communication to global structure, and the rise of JEPA
sections.summary: This section reviews three related areas: swarm learning that extracts global information from local communication, multi-agent representation learning for coordination, and JEPA shifting away from raw observation reconstruction. It positions this work at their intersection.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into three lines:

- **Extracting global information from local interactions**: Permutation-invariant encoders, graph neural networks (GNNs), and global-state prediction (GSP) have demonstrated that the hidden macroscopic structure of a swarm can be recovered through local message passing. This paper takes that concept further, focusing on a more precise and measurable problem: can each individual independently predict the same future collective target?

- **Multi-agent predictive representations**: Frameworks like MASIA, TIMAR, and recent decentralized world models aim to improve communication and cooperative behavior via future prediction. However, these are often evaluated through cumulative reward or emergent communication, without isolating and measuring future collective states directly as endpoints in terms of accuracy and inter-robot agreement.

- **Expanding JEPA beyond single observations**: JEPA avoids wasting capacity on reconstructing pixel-level noise, predicting instead within a task-relevant latent space. While JEPA has begun expanding to multi-agent settings such as collective-level JEPA, vehicle-to-everything (V2X-JEPA), and trajectory prediction (TrajJEPA), prior approaches assumed centralized pooling or fusion. CS-JEPA addresses the complementary, unexplored challenge of training all robots to independently predict the same size-invariant future through a fixed decentralized interface.

sections.heading: Defining a shared future target in a decentralized world
sections.summary: The paper formalizes the constraints on local observations and communication. Without directly sharing or averaging predictions, all robots independently predict the identical size-invariant latent target $Z_{t+h}$.
sections.details:
A central simulator or server can easily compute the global future. The challenge here is making that future predictable from diverse local information sets without distributing (copying back) a central estimate to the robots.

At time $t$, the swarm is modeled as a dynamic graph $\mathcal{G}_t = (\mathcal{V}_t, \mathcal{E}_t)$. A robot $i$'s local observation $o_t^i$ contains only its normalized coordinates, velocity, task vector (goal heading or relative displacement to a target), and an active flag. Raw neighbor features are completely hidden; robots only communicate their previous-step hidden states (64-dimensional float) with neighbors. Future action information and episode clocks are also masked.

The goal is to define a single permutation-invariant future target $Z_{t+h}$ for the whole swarm while having each robot $i$ produce an independent prediction $\widehat{Z}_{t+h}^{\,,i}$ using only its own history. Predictions are never averaged, testing whether each robot can construct the shared future entirely on its own. For evaluation, small linear probes are trained on frozen features to decode 10 physical collective variables, including polarization, connectivity, collision fraction, and task score.

Communication is strictly capped at 256 bytes per directed edge (64 float32 values). By mean-pooling neighbor messages, the GRU input tensor width remains constant regardless of neighborhood size. This ensures the computational cost of the entire network scales locally.

sections.heading: An architecture for fixed-size latent futures and local messaging
sections.summary: This section details CS-JEPA's network design and training scheme: a size-invariant latent target of 17 fixed tokens, a self-supervised loss with zero agreement loss, and a capacity-matched raw-reconstruction baseline (Future-Recon).
sections.details:
The key components of the approach are:

- **Recurrent local message passing**: Each robot encodes its observation and passes it along with the mean-pooled neighbor hidden states into a GRU, updating its own hidden state. Across a 16-frame history, messages naturally propagate across multiple hops. At test time, robots cannot inspect each other's predictions.

- **Size-invariant future target (tokenizer)**: To keep target dimensionality constant regardless of robot count, a fixed tokenizer extracts 17 tokens from the swarm: 1 global token and a $4 \times 4$ spatial grid of 16 anchor tokens (65 dimensions each, totaling 1105 dimensions). As a result, the target width is fixed at 1105 dimensions across any swarm size $N$.

- **Loss function formulation**: The predictor forecasts latent targets at horizons $t+2$ and $t+4$. Crucially, the agreement loss weight penalizing prediction differences across robots is set strictly to zero. Every robot is trained independently toward the shared target $Z_{t+h}$, with no cross-robot gradient flow directly matching their outputs. To prevent robots from losing track of their own local dynamics, an auxiliary local anchor loss (weight $\lambda=2$) predicting the robot's own future features is included during training only.

- **Fair baseline (Future-Recon)**: To isolate the benefit of predicting latent representations, the authors designed Future-Recon, matching CS-JEPA in backbone, communication bandwidth, and deployment parameter count (123,713 parameters). Instead of predicting latent features, Future-Recon reconstructs raw positions, velocities, and task vectors (119 dimensions total) across future spatial bins. This ensures that any performance gap is strictly due to predicting in latent space rather than architectural differences.

sections.heading: Fair comparisons and rigorous leak prevention
sections.summary: This section covers experimental tasks (flocking, formation, coverage), rigorous generalization tests under topology and swarm-size shifts, low-label linear probing (6 to 24 episodes), and leak-prevention protocols.
sections.details:
Experiments are conducted across three tasks: flocking, formation, and coverage. Models are trained on small-world communication graphs with $N \in \{10, 18\}$, then subjected to unseen distribution shifts during evaluation:
- **Topology shifts**: Unseen communication structures such as ring graphs and mutual-kNN graphs.
- **Size shifts**: Large swarms of $N \in \{36, 72, 108\}$, up to 6x the training sizes.

In probing evaluations, the learned representations are frozen, and ridge regression probes are trained using global labels from only 6, 12, or 24 episodes. The metrics evaluated are Accuracy MSE (normalized decoding error across 10 physical variables) and Agreement MSE (prediction discrepancy among robots within the same episode), assessed via the area under the curve (AUC) across the training curves.

To ensure scientific rigor, downstream collective labels remain completely hidden during pretraining. Strict controls are also put in place: a translation-free ablation that removes shared origin coordinates to prevent shortcut learning, and a crossed pretraining control that swaps the stage-0 encoder pretraining objectives.

sections.heading: Predictions align without agreement loss, and accuracy surges
sections.summary: Across all 12 independent seeds, CS-JEPA dramatically improved both prediction agreement and accuracy over Future-Recon. It also enhanced decision quality in counterfactual value estimation and closed-loop rigid-body control.
sections.details:
Key empirical findings include:

- **Emergence of agreement without agreement loss**: Despite an agreement loss weight of zero, inter-robot prediction discrepancy decreased across all evaluated data splits and all 12 independent random seeds ($p=0.000488$). Crucially, prediction accuracy AUC improved on the exact same seeds and splits: collective-state decoding error dropped by 28.4% in-distribution (ID) and by 64.4 to 75.6% under topology and swarm-size shifts. This completely rules out representation collapse, where robots trivially agree by predicting an uninformative constant.

- **Ruling out coordinate and encoder artifacts**: In the translation-free setting—where robots cannot share an origin or target displacement—CS-JEPA maintained its advantage in both accuracy (18.1% improvement) and agreement (52.4% improvement). Furthermore, when pretraining the stage-0 encoder with raw reconstruction, CS-JEPA's superiority persisted, proving that predicting latent targets in stage 1 is the decisive factor.

- **Counterfactual value estimation**: When conditioned on 4-step action plans, CS-JEPA improved value MSE and Pearson correlation across 8/8 seeds, not only on training swarm sizes but also on an unseen $N=32$ configuration (Table V).

- **Fully decentralized rigid-body control**: In 240Hz physics simulations of Crazyflie cf2x drones under severe communication impairments (20% packet loss, latency, and jitter), each robot autonomously selected and executed plans from its local predictions. This yielded a 5.3% utility gain over Future-Recon (outperforming it in 12/16 seeds) and substantially beat fixed-parameter standard control across all 16/16 seeds (Table VI).

sections.heading: Why does it work, and what questions remain?
sections.summary: This section analyzes why predicting abstract collective structure rather than raw details aids decentralized consensus, while candidly discussing limitations such as simulation-only testing and shared orientation assumptions.
sections.details:
Why do predictions align without explicit consensus training? The sole difference between CS-JEPA and Future-Recon is whether the target is raw observations or a learned latent representation. When reconstructing raw observations, each robot is forced to guess fine-grained local noise and unobserved details, leading independent predictions to diverge. In contrast, latent targets preserve core collective properties (such as center of mass and overall flocking flow) while discarding irrelevant local noise, making it easier for fragmented views to arrive at the same global future.

However, the paper acknowledges several clear limitations:
- **Simulation-only evaluation**: Experiments have not yet been validated on real physical hardware, leaving real-world sensor noise and asynchronous communication for future work.
- **Coordinate frame assumptions**: While translation invariance was demonstrated, robots are still assumed to share a common orientation and metric scale.
- **Value estimation vs. regret gap**: Although counterfactual value estimation became more accurate, this improvement did not directly reduce decision regret (the gap relative to the optimal plan) during online action selection.

sections.heading: One future: A new path toward decentralized swarm intelligence
sections.summary: CS-JEPA demonstrates that decentralized robot representations naturally align by predicting the same latent future, without forcing consensus. This opens up a promising paradigm for multi-robot coordination without centralized communication or output pooling.
sections.details:
The conclusion of this study is straightforward: rather than commanding robots to agree with each other via an agreement loss, simply training each robot to predict the same abstract future naturally aligns their predictions and dramatically boosts physical accuracy, even when they only possess fragmented local evidence.

CS-JEPA offers a scalable design where communication bandwidth and representation dimensions do not grow with swarm size, high label efficiency allowing collective variables to be probed from minimal data, and robust generalization to unseen topologies and scales. These traits form a practical foundation for large-scale decentralized swarm robotics, highlighting shared latent future targets as a powerful tool for cognitive alignment in distributed systems.

takeaways: Independent predictions naturally align without pooling or averaging, simply by having each robot predict a shared latent-space target (JEPA)
Compared to raw observation reconstruction, latent future prediction is dramatically more robust to unseen topologies and swarm sizes up to 6x larger (reducing error by 64 to 75%)
A fixed-width tokenizer (1 global + 16 spatial grid tokens) keeps communication bandwidth and representation dimensions strictly constant (size-invariant) as robot count grows

Decoding accuracy across 10 physical collective variables (e.g., connectivity, polarization) improves alongside agreement, confirming that useful information is preserved without representation collapse
limitations: Evaluations remain confined to simulation environments such as PyBullet; real-world hardware tests under actual packet drops and sensor noise are left for future work
Robots are assumed to share a common orientation and metric scale, meaning fully arbitrary local coordinate systems are not yet addressed
While offline counterfactual value estimation accuracy improved, it did not directly translate to lower regret in chosen plans during online decision-making
